title: Metabolic Adaptation in Disease States
objectives: Explain how chronic diseases alter normal metabolic pathways
Identify characteristic metabolic signatures of pathological states
Describe compensatory mechanisms during metabolic stress
Recognize therapeutic targets in disease-induced metabolic dysfunction

cancer_metabolism.title: Cancer (Warburg Effect)
cancer_metabolism.content:
Aerobic Glycolysis
• Key feature: ↑Lactate production despite O2 availability
• Enzymes upregulated: HK-II, PKM2, LDHA
• Purpose: Biosynthetic precursors (nucleotides, lipids)

Clinical Implications

Diagnosis: 18F-FDG PET scans exploit ↑glucose uptake

Therapy: Dichloroacetate (PDK inhibitor) trials

sepsis_metabolism.title: Sepsis (Hypercatabolic State)
sepsis_metabolism.content:
Phase 1: Cytokine Storm

  • ↑Proteolysis (Ubiquitin-proteasome pathway)
  • ↑Lipolysis (Hormone-sensitive lipase activation)
  • Insulin resistance (TNF-α mediated)

Phase 2: Immunoparalysis

  • ↓Oxidative phosphorylation
  • Mitochondrial dysfunction
  • Lactic acidosis (Type B)

obesity_adaptations.title: Morbid Obesity
obesity_adaptations.content:
Adipose Tissue Dysfunction
• Pathologic secretions:
- ↑Leptin (but resistant)
- ↓Adiponectin
- ↑IL-6/TNF-α
• Result: Systemic inflammation

NAFLD Progression

Steatosis → NASH: Lipotoxicity from ↑FFA flux

Marker: ↑AST/ALT ratio >1 (advanced fibrosis)

clinical_relevance.title: Therapeutic Targets
clinical_relevance.content:
Cancer Metabolism Drugs

Hexokinase inhibitor: 2-Deoxyglucose

Glutamine antagonist: DON (6-Diazo-5-oxo-L-norleucine)

Sepsis Nutrition

Key strategy: Permissive hypocaloric feeding

Supplement: Ω-3 fatty acids (anti-inflammatory)

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Why do cancer cells avoid oxidative phosphorylation?

Glycolysis provides rapid ATP and critical biosynthetic intermediates (ribose-5-P for nucleotides, NADPH for lipid synthesis) needed for rapid proliferation, despite being less energy-efficient.

How does sepsis cause both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia?

Early sepsis induces stress hyperglycemia (cortisol/catecholamines), while late-stage hepatic dysfunction impairs gluconeogenesis, causing hypoglycemia - a poor prognostic sign.

Why does ketosis preserve muscle mass in starvation?

Ketones replace glucose as the brain's primary fuel, reducing gluconeogenic demand for amino acids from muscle proteolysis (sparing ~30g protein/day).
